title: What is AI?
def: Software that performs tasks which normally need human intelligence — recognizing images, understanding language, making decisions.
note: AI is the umbrella term. Machine learning, LLMs and agents are all specific approaches inside it, not synonyms for it.

title: What is machine learning?
def: A way of building AI where the system learns patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed with rules.
note: Show it enough labeled examples, and it learns the pattern itself — that's the shift from classic programming to ML.

title: What is an LLM?
def: A Large Language Model — a neural network trained on huge amounts of text, so it can read and generate language.
note: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are all products built around an LLM. The LLM is the model; the product is the model plus an interface.

title: What is an AI agent?
def: An LLM that can take actions, not just reply with text — it can call tools, check results and decide what to do next.
note: A plain chatbot only talks. An agent can act: search the web, run code, call an API, then use what it finds to keep going.

title: What is a "model" in AI?
def: The trained system itself — millions or billions of numbers (parameters) that turn an input into an output.
note: "Model" is the generic term; an LLM is one kind of model, specifically one trained on language.

title: What is a prompt?
def: The text you give the model as input — an instruction, a question, or both.
note: Prompting is how you steer a model without changing its underlying weights. Same model, different prompt, different behavior.

title: Training vs inference — what's the difference?
def: Training is when the model learns from data, once, at huge cost. Inference is every time you actually use it afterward.
note: When you chat with a model, you're doing inference. The model's knowledge was fixed back when it was trained.

title: What is a hallucination in AI?
def: When a model states something false or made-up as if it were fact, with no signal that it's unsure.
note: It happens because the model is predicting plausible-sounding text, not looking facts up — confidence and correctness aren't the same thing.

title: Function calling / tool use
def: The model doesn't run code — it emits a structured request to call a function you defined, and your code runs it.
note: You describe each tool as a schema; the model replies with the name and arguments to invoke. This is the bridge from chat to action.

title: Token
def: The smallest chunk of text a model reads or writes — usually a word-piece, not a whole word.
note: Everything is counted, priced and limited in tokens. For English, ~4 characters is about 1 token.
code: tokens = ["token", "izing"]   # "tokenizing" -> 2 tokens, not 1 word

title: Context window
def: The maximum number of tokens a model can hold in view at once — your prompt and its reply combined.
note: Anything outside it is invisible. Overflow means the oldest tokens fall off or must be summarized.
code:
used = prompt_tokens + reply_tokens
assert used <= context_window   # or it overflows

title: Temperature
def: How random the model's sampling is. Low keeps it focused and repeatable; high makes it diverse and creative.
note: Near 0 it's almost deterministic — good for extraction. Raise it for brainstorming.
code: { "temperature": 0.2, "top_p": 1.0 }

title: Chat messages
def: Modern LLM APIs take a list of role-tagged messages, not a single prompt string.
note: system sets behaviour, user asks, assistant answers — and the whole history is resent every turn.

title: Embedding
def: Text turned into a fixed-length vector, so meaning becomes a distance you can measure.
note: Similar meanings land near each other — the basis for search, clustering and retrieval.

title: Self-attention
def: Every token looks at every other token and weighs how relevant it is — that's how context flows through the model.
note: Query x Key produces the weights; those weights mix the Values. It's the heart of the transformer.
code:
scores  = query @ key.T
weights = softmax(scores)
out     = weights @ value

title: Transformer
def: The architecture behind modern LLMs: stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers, with no recurrence.
note: It processes a whole sequence in parallel, which is why it trains and scales so well.

title: Positional encoding
def: Attention is order-blind on its own, so each token's position is baked into its vector.
note: Without it, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical to the model.

title: Softmax
def: Turns raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1.
note: It's the final step that decides how likely each possible next token is.
code: probs = exp(logits) / sum(exp(logits))   # sums to 1

title: Next-token prediction
def: An LLM only ever does one thing: predict the probability of the next token, sample one, and repeat.
note: Everything else — chat, code, reasoning — emerges from doing this well, one token at a time.
code:
logits  = model(tokens)
next_id = sample(softmax(logits), temperature=0.7)

title: ReAct (reason + act)
def: The model thinks, calls a tool, reads the result, then thinks again — interleaving reasoning with action.
note: Each step is grounded in a real observation instead of one long guessed-at answer.
code:
Thought: I need today's weather.
Action: get_weather("Alicante")
Observation: 29C, clear skies
Thought: Now I can answer.

title: The agent loop
def: An agent is a loop: think, act, observe, repeat — until the goal is met or a step limit is hit.
note: The loop plus tools plus memory is what turns a plain chat model into an agent.
code:
while not done:
    action = model.decide(state)
    result = run(action)
    state  = update(state, result)
    done   = action.is_final

title: Memory
def: Short-term memory is the context window; long-term memory is external storage you retrieve into it.
note: Agents summarize or store past steps so they don't forget once the window fills up.

title: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
def: Fetch relevant documents and drop them into the prompt, so the model answers from facts rather than only its training.
note: Cuts hallucination and lets a model use private or fresh data it never saw during training.
code:
docs   = retrieve(query, top_k=4)
prompt = context(docs) + query
answer = model(prompt)

title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
def: An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through one consistent interface.
note: Write a connector once and any MCP-aware client can use it — a bit like a USB port for tools.

title: What is an AI skill?
def: A folder of instructions and resources — templates, scripts, checklists — that a model reads before doing a task. Packaged know-how, loaded on demand.
note: A skill teaches the model HOW (it reads, then does the work itself); MCP gives it ACCESS to live systems. Runbook vs phone line — full comparison on the MCP vs REST page.
code:
flowchart LR
    F[Skill folder]:::n -->|read into context| M[Model]:::n -->|does the work itself| R[Result]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Evals
def: Systematic tests that score model or agent output, so you can tell whether a change actually helped.
note: Without evals you're tuning by vibes; with them, progress becomes measurable.
code: score = sum(check(model(x)) for x in test_set) / len(test_set)

title: What is an agent workflow?
def: A graph of steps an agent system runs through — not one long prompt, but a structured, typed sequence you can inspect and control.
note: This is what separates a serious agent framework from a chat loop: the orchestration itself becomes a first-class, strongly-typed object instead of hidden inside one big prompt.

title: Executors and edges — the building blocks of a workflow
def: An executor is one unit of work in a workflow — an agent or a plain function. An edge is the connection that routes output from one executor to the next.
note: Edges can fan out to run several executors in parallel, fan in to combine their results, or route conditionally based on what came out of the previous step.

title: What is checkpointing in an agent workflow?
def: Saving a workflow's state mid-run, so it can be paused, killed, or crash — and resume later from exactly where it left off, not from the start.
note: This is what makes long-running or expensive agent workflows practical: a multi-hour task survives a restart instead of burning every token again.

title: What is handoff orchestration?
def: A multi-agent pattern where a triage agent routes a request to the right specialist agent, and any specialist can hand the conversation back or sideways if it turns out to be the wrong fit.
note: The developer defines the topology — which agents exist and who can hand off to whom — but the agents themselves decide, in the moment, when a handoff is needed.

title: What is an agent harness?
def: A ready-made shell around a model that turns it into a working coding agent in one step — file access, task tracking, shell execution, and approvals, all pre-wired.
note: Instead of hand-building memory, file tools, and a sandbox yourself, a harness gives you the standard agent scaffolding out of the box.

title: What is agent-to-agent (A2A) communication?
def: A protocol that lets independent agents send each other structured messages, even across different frameworks or programming languages.
note: This is how a .NET agent and a Python agent — built by different teams on different stacks — can still delegate work to one another reliably.

title: Harness engineering
def: Designing the environment an agent acts inside — its sandbox, its file system access, and the runtime surface it's allowed to touch.
note: A harness decides what's even possible for the agent to attempt. No amount of clever prompting fixes a missing file permission or a shell it can't reach.
code:
flowchart TD
    A[Agent]:::n --> H[Harness]:::n
    H --> SB[Sandbox]:::n
    H --> FS[File system]:::n
    H --> RT[Runtime surface]:::n
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px

title: Loop engineering
def: Deciding when the agent takes another step and when it stops — the control logic wrapped around think, act, observe.
note: Stop too early and the task is unfinished. Stop too late and you burn tokens on a loop that already found its answer three steps ago.
code:
flowchart TD
    T[Think]:::n --> Ac[Act]:::n --> O[Observe]:::n
    O -->|not done| T
    O -->|done| S([Stop]):::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Context engineering
def: Curating what actually lands in the context window on each turn — pulling in what's relevant, and actively keeping out what isn't.
note: Most 'prompt engineering' problems that show up in production are really context problems: too much irrelevant history, not too few clever words.
code:
flowchart TD
    H[History]:::n --> Sel[Selector]:::n
    Tl[Tool output]:::n --> Sel
    M[Memory]:::n --> Sel
    Sel --> W[Context window]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Tool design
def: Writing the tool itself, not just its call schema — an agent's ceiling is what its tools let it do, and its risk is their worst edge case.
note: A tool that fails silently or accepts unchecked input hands the agent a way to cause real damage without anyone actually deciding it should be allowed to.
code:
flowchart TD
    C[Model call]:::n --> Sc[Tool schema]:::n --> V[Validate]:::n --> Ex[Execute]:::ok --> R[Result]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Memory architecture
def: The design decisions behind what an agent remembers, for how long, and what it's allowed to forget.
note: Not everything belongs in long-term storage — a well-designed architecture decides what gets promoted from a single run into something durable.
code:
flowchart TD
    C[Context window]:::n -->|fills up| Su[Summarize / evict]:::n
    Su --> L[Long-term store]:::ok
    L -->|retrieve| C
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Orchestration patterns
def: The shape of an agent system — one agent, a planner delegating to workers, or a swarm of peers — and each shape fails differently.
note: A single agent fails by running out of context. A swarm fails by agents stepping on each other's work. Pick the shape for the failure mode you can live with.
code:
flowchart TD
    P[Planner]:::n --> W1[Worker A]:::n
    P --> W2[Worker B]:::n
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px

title: Guardrails & permissions
def: The checks that run before an agent's action executes, and what happens when the action it wants to take isn't allowed.
note: A guardrail that only logs a violation after the fact isn't a guardrail — it has to be able to block or reroute before the action actually runs.
code:
flowchart TD
    A[Agent action]:::n --> P{Policy check}:::n
    P -->|allowed| E[Execute]:::ok
    P -->|denied| B[Block / ask human]:::warn
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px
    classDef warn fill:#FBE7E7,stroke:#B23B3B,color:#8C2323,font-size:13px

title: Evals for agents
def: Scoring an agent's whole trajectory — every step it took — not just whether the final output looks right.
note: Two runs can land on the same correct answer through very different paths, and one of those paths might have touched something it shouldn't have.
code:
flowchart TD
    S1[Step 1]:::n --> S2[Step 2]:::n --> S3[Step N]:::n --> F[Final answer]:::n
    F -.-> Sc[Trajectory score]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Human-in-the-loop design
def: Deciding upfront which categories of decision never get delegated to the agent, no matter how confident it is.
note: The line isn't drawn per-request in the moment — it's drawn in the design, before the agent is ever capable of proposing that action.
code:
flowchart TD
    A[Agent proposes]:::n --> D{High-stakes?}:::n
    D -->|no| Au[Auto-run]:::ok
    D -->|yes| H[Human approves]:::warn --> Ex[Execute]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px
    classDef warn fill:#FBE7E7,stroke:#B23B3B,color:#8C2323,font-size:13px

title: Observability & tracing
def: Recording every step an agent takes — inputs, outputs, timing, tool calls — so a failure deep in a run is inspectable, not a black box.
note: When a 30-step run breaks at step 14, a trace lets you look straight at step 14, instead of re-running the whole thing and guessing where it went wrong.
code:
flowchart TD
    R[Run: steps 1-30]:::n -->|logs every step| T[Trace log]:::n
    T --> J[Jump to step 14]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px
